entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.1-2Sam.12.4">2Sa 12:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen4388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4389" type="x-p"/> Nathan’s Reproof. - 2Sa 12:1. To ensure the success of his mission, viz., to charge the king with his crimes, Nathan resorted to a parable by which he led on the king to pronounce sentence of death upon himself. The parable is a very simple one, and drawn from life. Two men were living in a certain city: the one was rich, and had many sheep and oxen; the other was poor, and possessed nothing at all but one small lamb which he had bought and nourished (יחיּה, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. kept alive), so that it grew up in his house along with his son, and was treated most tenderly and loved like a daughter. The custom of keeping pet-sheep in the house, as we keep lap-dogs, is still met with among the Arabs (vid., Bochart, <hi type="italic">Hieroz</hi>. i. p. 594). There came a traveller (הלך, a journey, for a traveller) to the rich man (לאישׁ without an article, the express definition being introduced afterwards in connection with the adjective העשׁיר; vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §293 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, p. 741), and he grudged to take of his own sheep and oxen to prepare (sc., a meal) for the traveller who had come to his house; “and he took the poor man’s lamb, and dressed it for the man that had come to him.”

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.5-2Sam.12.6">2Sa 12:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen4389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4390" type="x-p"/> David was so enraged at this act of violence on the part of the rich man, that in the heat of his anger he pronounced this sentence at once: <hi type="italic">“As the Lord liveth, the man who did this deserves to die; and the lamb he shall restore fourfold.”</hi> The fourfold restoration corresponds to the law in Exo 22:1. The culprit himself was also to be put to death, because the forcible robbery of a poor man’s pet-lamb was almost as bad as man-stealing.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.7-2Sam.12.8">2Sa 12:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen4390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4391" type="x-p"/> The parable was so selected that David could not suspect that it had reference to him and to his son. With all the greater shock therefore did the words of the prophet, <hi type="italic">“Thou art the man,”</hi> come upon the king. Just as in the parable the sin is traced to its root - namely, insatiable covetousness - so now, in the words of Jehovah which follow, and in which the prophet charges the king directly with his crime, he brings out again in the most unsparing manner this hidden background of all sins, for the purpose of bringing thoroughly home to his heart the greatness of his iniquity, and the condemnation it deserved. <hi type="italic">“Jehovah the God of Israel hath said, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul, and I gave thee thy master’s house and thy master’s wives into thy bosom.”</hi> These words refer to the fact that, according to the general custom in the East, when a king died, his successor upon the throne also succeeded to his harem, so that David was at liberty to take his predecessor’s wives; though we cannot infer from this that he actually did so: in fact this is by no means probable, since, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.50">1Sa 14:50</reference>, Saul had but one wife, and according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.7">2Sa 3:7</reference> only one concubine, whom Abner appropriated to himself. <hi type="italic">“And gave thee the house of Israel and Judah;”</hi> i.e., I handed over the whole nation to thee as king, so that thou couldst have chosen young virgins as wives from all the daughters of Judah and Israel. מעט ואם, <hi type="italic">“and if </hi>(all this was) <hi type="italic">too little, I would have added to thee this and that.”</hi>

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.9">2Sa 12:9</reference> <hi type="italic">“Why hast thou despised the word of Jehovah, to do evil in His eyes? Thou hast slain Uriah the Hethite with the sword, and taken his wife to be thy wife, and slain him with the sword of the Ammonites.”</hi> The last clause does not contain any tautology, but serves to strengthen the thought by defining more sharply the manner in which David destroyed Uriah. הרג, to murder, is stronger than הכּה; and the fact that it was by the sword of <hi type="italic">the Ammonites</hi>, the enemies of the people of God, that the deed was done, added to the wickedness.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.10-2Sam.12.12">2Sa 12:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen4391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4392" type="x-p"/> The punishment answers to the sin. There is first of all (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.10">2Sa 12:10</reference>) the punishment for the murder of Uriah: <hi type="italic">“The sword shall not depart from thy house for ever, because thou hast despised me, and hast taken the wife,”</hi> etc. <hi type="italic">“For ever”</hi> must not be toned down to the indefinite idea of a long period, but must be held firmly in its literal signification. the expression “thy house,” however, does not refer to the house of David as continued in his descendants, but simply as existing under David himself until it was broken up by his death. The fulfilment of this threat commenced with the murder of Amnon by Absalom (<reference osisRef="2Sam.13.29">2Sa 13:29</reference>); it was continued in the death of Absalom the rebel (<reference osisRef="2Sam.18.14">2Sa 18:14</reference>), and was consummated in the execution of Adonijah (1Ki 2:24-25).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.13-2Sam.12.14">2Sa 12:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen4393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4394" type="x-p"/> These words went to David’s heart, and removed the ban of hardening which pressed upon it. He confessed to the prophet, <hi type="italic">“I have sinned against the Lord.”</hi> “The words are very few, just as in the case of the publican in the Gospel of Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.13">Luk 18:13</reference>). But that is a good sign of a thoroughly broken spirit ...  There is no excuse, no cloaking, no palliation of the sin. There is no searching for a loophole, ... no pretext put forward, no human weakness pleaded. He acknowledges his guilt openly, candidly, and without prevarication” (<hi type="italic">Berleb. Bible</hi>). In response to this candid confession of his sin, Nathan announced to him, <hi type="italic">“The Lord also hath let thy sin pass by </hi>(i.e., forgiven it)<hi type="italic">. Thou wilt not die. Only because by this deed thou hast given the enemies of the Lord occasion to blaspheme, the son that is born unto thee shall die.”</hi> נאץ, inf. abs. Piel, with chirek, because of its similarity in sound to the following perfect (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §240, <hi type="italic">c</hi>.). גּם, with which the apodosis commences, belongs to the הבּן which follows, and serves to give emphasis to the expression: “Nevertheless the son” (vid., Ges<hi type="italic">.</hi> §155, 2, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.). David himself had deserved to die as an adulterer and murderer. The Lord remitted the punishment of death, not so much because of his heartfelt repentance, as from His own fatherly grace and compassion, and because of the promise that He had given to David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.11-2Sam.7.12">2Sa 7:11-12</reference>), - a promise which rested upon the assumption that David would not altogether fall away from a state of grace, or commit a mortal sin, but that even in the worst cases he would turn to the Lord again and seek forgiveness. The Lord therefore punished him for this sin with the judgments announced in <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.10-2Sam.12.12">2Sa 12:10-12</reference>, as about to break upon him and his house. But as his sin had given occasion to the enemies of the Lord - i.e., not only to the heathen, but also to the unbelieving among the Israelites themselves - to blaspheme or ridicule his religion and that of all other believers also, the child that was begotten in adultery and had just been born should die; in order, on the one hand, that the father should atone for his adultery in the death of the son, and, on the other hand, that the visible occasion for any further blasphemy should be taken away: so that David was not only to feel the pain of punishment in the death of his son, but was also to discern in it a distinct token of the grace of God. <div eID="gen4394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4395" type="x-p"/> David’s Penitential Grief, and the Birth of Solomon. - 2Sa 12:15. The last-mentioned punishment was inflicted without delay. When Nathan had gone home, the Lord smote the child, so that it became very ill.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.16-2Sam.12.17">2Sa 12:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen4395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4396" type="x-p"/> Then David sought God (in prayer) for the boy, and fasted, and went and lay all night upon the earth. וּבא, <hi type="italic">“he came,”</hi> not into the sanctuary of the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.20">2Sa 12:20</reference> is proof to the contrary), but into his house, or into his chamber, to pour out his heart before God, and bend beneath His chastising hand, and refused the appeal of his most confidential servants, who tried to raise him up, and strengthen him with food. <hi type="italic">“The elders of his house,”</hi> judging from <reference osisRef="Gen.24.2">Gen 24:2</reference>, were the oldest and most confidential servants, “the most highly honoured of his servants, and those who had the greatest influence with him” (Clericus).

When they answered in the affirmative, he rose up from the ground, washed and anointed himself, and changed his clothes; that is to say, he laid aside all the signs of penitential grief and mourning, went into the house of the Lord (the holy tent upon Mount Zion) and worshipped, and then returned to his house, and had food set before him.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.21-2Sam.12.22">2Sa 12:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen4398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4399" type="x-p"/> When his servants expressed their astonishment at all this, David replied, <hi type="italic">“As long as the boy lived, I fasted and wept: for I thought </hi>(said), <hi type="italic">Perhaps </hi>(who knows) <hi type="italic">the Lord may be gracious to me, that the child may remain alive. But now he is dead, why should I fast? can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me.”</hi> On this O. v. Gerlach has the following admirable remarks: “In the case of a man whose penitence was so earnest and so deep, the prayer for the preservation of his child must have sprung from some other source than excessive love of any created object. His great desire was to avert the stroke, as a sign of the wrath of God, in the hope that he might be able to discern, in the preservation of the child, a proof of divine favour consequent upon the restoration of his fellowship with God. But when the child was dead, he humbled himself under the mighty hand of God, and rested satisfied with His grace, without giving himself up to fruitless pain.” This state of mind is fully explained in Ps 51, though his servants could not comprehend it. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.23-2Sam.12.25">2Sa 12:23-25</reference> <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.12.23">2Sa 12:23</reference></hi> is paraphrased very correctly by Clericus: “I shall go to the dead, the dead will not come to me.” - 2Sa 12:24. David then comforted his wife Bathsheba, and lived with her again; and she bare a son, whom he called <hi type="italic">Solomon</hi>, the man of peace (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.9">1Ch 22:9</reference>). David gave the child this name, because he regarded his birth as a pledge that he should now become a partaker again of peace with God, and not from any reference to the fact that the war with the Ammonites was over, and peace prevailed when he was born; although in all probability Solomon was not born till after the capture of Rabbah and the termination of the Ammonitish war. His birth is mentioned here simply because of its connection with what immediately precedes. The writer adds (in <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.24">2Sa 12:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.25">2Sa 12:25</reference>), <hi type="italic">“And Jehovah loved him, and sent by the hand </hi>(through the medium)<hi type="italic">of Nathan the prophet; and he called his son Jedidiah</hi> (i.e., beloved of Jehovah), <hi type="italic">for Jehovah’s sake.”</hi> The subject to ויּשׁלח (he sent) cannot be David, because this would not yield any appropriate sense, but must be <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, the subject of the clause immediately preceding. “To send by the hand,” i.e., to make a mission by a person (vid., <reference osisRef="Exod.4.13">Exo 4:13</reference>, etc.), is equivalent to having a commission performed by a person, or entrusting a person with a commission to another. We learn from what follows, in what the commission with which Jehovah entrusted Nathan consisted: <hi type="italic">“And he </hi>(Nathan, not Jehovah)<hi type="italic">called his </hi>(the boy’s) <hi type="italic">name Jedidiah.”</hi> And if Nathan is the subject to “called,” there is nothing to astonish in the expression “because of the Lord.” The idea is this: Nathan came to David according to Jehovah’s instructions, and gave Solomon the name <hi type="italic">Jedidiah</hi> for Jehovah’s sake, i.e., because Jehovah loved him. The giving of such a name was a practical declaration on the part of Jehovah that He loved Solomon, from which David could and was intended to discern that the Lord had blessed his marriage with Bathsheba. <hi type="italic">Jedidiah</hi>, therefore, was not actually adopted as Solomon’s name.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.26-2Sam.12.28">2Sa 12:26-28</reference> <div eID="gen4399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4400" type="x-p"/> Conquest of Rabbah, and Punishment of the Ammonites (comp. <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1-1Chr.20.3">1Ch 20:1-3</reference>). - <hi type="italic">“Joab fought against Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and took the king’s city.”</hi> המּלוּכה עיר, the capital of the kingdom, is the city with the exception of the acropolis, as <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.27">2Sa 12:27</reference> clearly shows, where the captured city is called “the water-city.” <hi type="italic">Rabbah</hi> was situated, as the ruins of <hi type="italic">Ammân</hi> show, on both banks of the river (<hi type="italic">Moiet</hi>) <hi type="italic">Ammân</hi> (the upper Jabbok), in a valley which is shut in upon the north and south by two bare ranges of hills of moderate height, and is not more than 200 paces in breadth. “The northern height is crowned by the castle, the ancient acropolis, which stands on the north-western side of the city, and commands the whole city” (see Burckhardt, <hi type="italic">Syria</hi> ii. pp. 612ff., and Ritter, <hi type="italic">Erdkunde</hi> xv. pp. 1145ff.). After taking the water-city, Joab sent messengers to David, to inform him of the result of the siege, and say to him, <hi type="italic">“Gather the rest of the people together, and besiege the city</hi> (i.e., the acropolis, which may have been peculiarly strong), <hi type="italic">and take it, that I may not take the city </hi>(also),<hi type="italic">and my name be named upon it,”</hi> i.e., the glory of the conquest be ascribed to me. Luther adopts this explanation in his free rendering, “and I have a name from it.”

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.30">2Sa 12:30</reference> <div eID="gen4401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4402" type="x-p"/> He then took their king’s crown (<hi type="italic">“their king,”</hi> viz., the king of the Ammonites) from off his (the king’s) head; so that he had either been taken prisoner or slain at the capture of the city. The weight of the crown was <hi type="italic">“a talent of gold, and precious stones”</hi> (sc., were upon it): as the writer of the Chronicles has correctly explained it by supplying בּהּ. The Hebrew talent (equal to 3000 shekels) was 83 1/2 Dresden pounds. But the strongest man could hardly have borne a crown of this weight upon his head for however short a time; and David could scarcely have placed it upon his own head. We must therefore assume that the account of the weight is not founded upon actual weighing, but simply upon an approximative estimate, which is somewhat too high. David also took a great quantity of booty out of the city. 1 Sa 12:31 <div eID="gen4402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4403" type="x-p"/> He also had the inhabitants executed, and that with cruel tortures. <hi type="italic">“He sawed them in pieces with the saw and with iron harrows.”</hi> בּמּגרה ויּשׂם, “he put them into the saw,” does not give any appropriate sense; and there can be no doubt, that instead of וישׂם we should read ויּשׂר (from שׂוּר): “he cut (sawed) them in pieces.” הבּרזל וּבמגזרות, <hi type="italic">“and with iron cutting tools.”</hi> The meaning of the ἁπ. λεγ. מגזרות cannot be more precisely determined. The current rendering, “axes or hatchets,” is simply founded upon the circumstance that גּזר, to cut, is applied in 2Ki 6:4 to the felling of trees. The reading in the Chronicles, וּבמּגרות, is evidently a copyist’s error, as we have already had בּמּגרה, “with the saw.” The meaning of the next clause is a disputed point, as the reading itself varies, and the Masoretes read בּמּלבּן instead of the <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> במלכן, “he made them go through brick-kilns,” i.e., burnt them in brick-kilns, as the lxx and Vulgate render it. On the other hand, Thenius takes the <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> under his protection, and adopts Kimchi’s explanation: “he led them through <hi type="italic">Malchan</hi>, i.e., through the place where the Ammonites burned their children in honour of their idol.” Thenius would therefore alter בּמלכּם into בּמלכּם or בּמּלכּם: “he offered them as sacrifices in their image of Moloch. ” But this explanation cannot be even grammatically sustained, to say nothing of the arbitrary character of the alteration proposed; for the technical expression למּלך בּאשׁ חעביר, “to cause to go through the fire for Moloch” (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">Lev 18:21</reference>), is essentially different from בּמּלך חעביר, to cause to pass through Moloch, an expression that we never meet with. Moreover, it is impossible to see how burning the Ammonites in the image of Moloch could possibly be “an obvious mode of punishing idolatry,” since the idolatry itself consisted in the fact that the Ammonites burned their children to Moloch. So far as the circumstances themselves are concerned, the cruelties inflicted upon the prisoners are not to be softened down, as Daaz and others propose, by an arbitrary perversion of the words into a mere sentence to hard labour, such as sawing wood, burning bricks, etc. At the same time, the words of the text do not affirm that <hi type="italic">all</hi> the inhabitants of Rabbah were put to death in this cruel manner. בּהּ אשׁר העם (without כּל) refers no doubt simply to the fighting men that were taken prisoners, or at the most to the male population of the acropolis of Rabbah, who probably consisted of fighting men only. In doing this, David merely retaliated upon the Ammonites the cruelties with which they had treated their foes; since according to <reference osisRef="Amos.1.13">Amo 1:13</reference> they ripped up women who were with child, and according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.2">1Sa 11:2</reference> their king Nahash would only make peace with the inhabitants of Jabesh upon the condition that the right eye of every one of them should be put out. It is sufficiently evident from this, that the Ammonites had aimed at the most shameful extermination of the Israelites. <hi type="italic">“Thus did he unto all the cities of the Ammonites,”</hi> i.e., to all the fortified cities that resisted the Israelites. After the close of this war, David returned to Jerusalem with all the men of war. The war with the Syrians and Ammonites, including as it did the Edomitish war as well, was the fiercest in which David was ever engaged, and was also the last great war of his life.  <chapter eID="2Sam.12"/> <div eID="gen4403" type="x-p"/>
